questions.q: Why can you restore a full backup and then jump straight to a differential backup, but not skip a log backup in the middle of a log chain?
options: A differential captures everything since the last full backup, while each log backup only covers the period since the previous log backup
Differentials and log backups are actually interchangeable, so order never matters
Log backups are always smaller, so skipping one has no effect on the chain
Differentials require RECOVERY while log backups require NORECOVERY
questions.explain: A differential is cumulative back to the last full, so no in-between differentials are needed. Log backups are not cumulative — each covers only since the previous log backup.

questions.q: What does WITH STOPAT do on a RESTORE LOG statement?
options: Applies log records only up to a specified date/time, instead of the entire log backup file
Stops the restore process entirely and rolls it back
Restores only the differential portion of a backup
Pauses the SQL Server Agent job that is running the restore
questions.explain: STOPAT lets you recover to an exact point in time within a log backup that spans that timestamp.

questions.q: In which recovery model(s) can WITH STOPAT point-in-time recovery actually work?
options: FULL or BULK_LOGGED, because SIMPLE recovery never retains a usable log to restore
SIMPLE only, since the log is always available there
It works identically in all three recovery models
Only in FULL, and never in BULK_LOGGED
questions.explain: SIMPLE recovery truncates the log automatically, so there's no log chain to restore for point-in-time recovery.

questions.q: Why does SQL Server refuse to apply a backup out of order during a restore sequence?
options: Each backup records an LSN (Log Sequence Number) range, and SQL Server rejects a backup whose range doesn't pick up where the database currently left off
SQL Server has no way to detect restore order and simply corrupts the database silently
Backups are encrypted with a sequence key that expires after 24 hours
It only checks the backup's file timestamp, not any internal sequence number
questions.explain: LSN ranges are how SQL Server validates that a backup logically continues from the database's current restored state.

questions.q: In a full → differential → two log backups restore sequence, which statement gets WITH RECOVERY instead of WITH NORECOVERY?
options: Only the very last statement in the sequence — the second log backup restore
Every statement in the sequence
Only the full backup restore
Only the differential backup restore
questions.explain: NORECOVERY is used on every step except the final one, which uses RECOVERY to bring the database online.
